catalog_quote: Stress is contrastive on the word level and is defined as a combination of pitch, and either length or intensity. There are two contranstive pitch levels, high and low. To mark stress, high pitch combines with increased intensity and low pitch combines with length. Note the four possible combinations on the following two syllable words: íko before, ikò sew, ìre food, and iré stand. Syllables vary in length then according to the stress pattern. In addition the initial syllable of any word may be given increased length for special emphasis. The phonological foot is a rhythmic segment composed of a nuclear syllable and zero to eight marginal syllables bounded by softened intensity and an optional pause. Secondary stress has been observed in the longer words but needs further analysis.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, locator (sec. 1.0, p.474, p.4) and the four accented disyllables are confirmed verbatim in the held sealang and its 400-dpi crop. (2) Deciding source: a 1975 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch by the language's principal fieldworker; Glottolog 5.1 lists no phonology publication for Barai, and the items typed 'grammar' are either Olson's syntax theses or mis-typed literacy booklets. I downloaded the four open works that could bear on it: Olson's 1981 ANU PhD (Appendix I p.336 restates contrastive stress realized as high pitch+intensity vs low pitch+length, adds 'functional load of minimal contrasts is light', gives further minimal pairs, and p.237 describes stress loss in compounds) -> confirms lexical; Dutton 1969 PL-B9 p.144 independently judged Barai stress 'probably phonemic' from variant stress positions -> confirms; Dutton 201

sources.citation: Olson, Michael Leon. 1981. Barai clause junctures: toward a functional theory of interclausal relations. PhD thesis, Australian National University. xii+374 leaves (392-pp scan). hdl:1885/110191.
sources.quote: p.336: 'Stress occurs contrastively either as high pitch and increased intensity (´) or as low pitch and length (`). The functional load of minimal contrasts is light however.' with minimal pairs íko 'going to eat' / ìko 'raw', irì 'sharpen' / irí 'stop'. p.237: in predicate compounds forming one phonological word 'one or the other of the predicates ... loses its pitch-stress' (fare high + fie low -> farefie with a single high pitch-stress on the initial syllable). Appendix states transcriptions follow Olson (1969) ms. 'Barai phonemics'.

sources.quote: Stress occurs contrastively either as high pitch and increased intensity (-) or as low pitch and length (·). The functional load of minimal contrasts is light however. iko [i.kho] 'going to eat' / iko [ikho] 'raw'; iri [i.ci] 'sharpen' / iri [i.cf.] 'stop'. [p. 336] ... One or the other of the predicates entering into the combination loses its pitch-stress. The sequence fare 'touch' with high pitch-stress on the first syllable and fie 'sense, hear, or understand' with low pitch-stress on the first syllable becomes farefie 'feel' with only a single high pitch-stress on the initial syllable. [pp. 236-237]

sources.quote: p.144: 'Insufficient time was spent on this aspect of the language to determine the status of stress in it. My impression is, however, that stress is probably phonemic since primary stress has variant positions in words of the same number of syllables, e.g., [moˈga] 'tanket (shrub)'; [ˈmisu] 'salt'.' p.135: 'None of the Koiarian languages is tonal.'

sources.note: A syntax thesis (tagmemic vs transformational analyses of phrase and clause).
